title: Same Accuracy, Twice As Fast: Continual Learning Surpasses Retraining From Scratch

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reframe continual learning for the unconstrained-memory setting, focusing on computational savings from reusing a trained model rather than only accuracy. Paper [6] discusses incremental learning as desirable for efficient resource usage, eliminating the need to retrain from scratch, which aligns with the computational savings aspect. Paper [12] also emphasizes reusing pretrained models to avoid retraining from scratch, targeting computational efficiency. Both papers share the same objective at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism introduces a novel evaluation framework that scores methods by compute reduction (L100/L99: relative iterations to match a fraction of the from-scratch model's final accuracy). Paper [21] introduces DAWNBench, a time-to-accuracy benchmark for machine learning performance, which evaluates training efficiency in terms of computational cost and accuracy trade-offs. This aligns with the primitive of measuring compute efficiency relative to accuracy. Paper [31] further analyzes the time-to-accuracy metric, reinforcing the equivalence in evaluation design.

### Evaluation
The evaluation framework defines L100 (compute to reach 100% of scratch accuracy) and uses naive continuous training as a baseline. Paper [21] uses DAWNBench, which similarly benchmarks compute efficiency and accuracy trade-offs, making the evaluation design covered. Paper [31] also analyzes the time-to-accuracy metric, confirming reuse of the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning in computer vision (image classification). Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], [6], [7], [10], [17], [24] all address continual learning in computer vision, including class-incremental and task-incremental settings. This general application area is well-covered.

**PURPOSE: Reframe continual learning for the practical (unconstrained-memory) setting where both old and new data are available, measuring computational savings from reusing a trained model rather than only accuracy.**

The key elements are: (1) continual learning setting, (2) unconstrained memory / full data access, (3) measuring *computational savings* from model reuse rather than accuracy. Paper [12] ("Reuse, Don't Retrain") explicitly addresses reusing a pretrained model to avoid training from scratch and focuses on computational cost savings. Paper [11] and [30] address warm-starting with full data access and note computational inefficiency. Paper [2] addresses continual learning with foundation models and computational cost. However, the specific framing of "reframe CL as a compute-savings problem when all data is available" is closest to [12], which explicitly frames the purpose as reusing a model to avoid the computational cost of retraining from scratch. Paper [30] ("On Warm-Starting Neural Network Training") directly studies the setting where old+new data are available and asks whether warm-starting saves compute — this is substantively equivalent to the purpose here. Paper [11] is the same paper essentially. These cover the purpose at the problem-class level.

---

**MECHANISM: Novel evaluation framework scoring methods by compute reduction (L100/L99 metric: relative iterations to match a fraction of scratch accuracy), with naive continue-training as reference.**

The L100/L99 metric is a specific "iterations-to-accuracy" style metric. Papers [21] and [31] introduce and analyze the DAWNBench "time-to-accuracy" benchmark, which measures training time/iterations needed to reach a target accuracy threshold. This is substantively the same primitive: measure compute (iterations/time) required to reach a fraction of a target accuracy. The L100 metric (iterations to reach X% of scratch final accuracy) is a direct instance of the time-to-accuracy design. Paper [14] also compares KD vs. scratch under a fixed compute budget, measuring accuracy at iso-compute. These cover the mechanism.

---

**EVALUATION: Framework defines L100; naive continuous training shown to converge slower; case study on CIFAR-100 70+30.**

The evaluation design uses a time-to-accuracy metric on an image classification benchmark (CIFAR-100), with a qualitative + case study approach. Papers [21] and [31] use the time-to-accuracy evaluation design on image classification benchmarks. The CIFAR-100 split benchmark is used in many continual learning papers (e.g., [1], [5], [6]). The evaluation design (time-to-accuracy on image classification) is covered by [21]/[31]. The case study / qualitative convergence comparison is a standard experimental shape. The specific CIFAR-100 70+30 split is a domain-level detail, not an evaluation design novelty.

---

**DOMAIN: Continual learning / computer vision (image classification).**

Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [10], [17], [24] all work in continual learning for image classification. This is clearly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to identify optimization aspects that can accelerate continual training when reusing an old model and provide concrete first-step methods for each. Papers [3], [4], [13], and [14] address related objectives in continual learning, such as improving adaptation efficiency, preventing catastrophic forgetting, and optimizing learning dynamics. However, none explicitly focus on identifying optimization aspects for accelerating continual training with reused models. Paper [10] discusses warm-starting neural network training, which is conceptually related but does not address the broader optimization aspect decomposition. Thus, no prior paper fully matches the purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism decomposes the problem into four aspects (initialization, regularization, data selection, hyper-parameters) and instantiates methods for each. Paper [1] and [2] propose L2-init regularization, which matches the regularization aspect. Paper [17] discusses difficulty-weighted learning, which aligns with the easy/hard replay sampling for data selection. Paper [9] and [10] discuss warm-starting and initialization strategies, which are conceptually similar to shrink-and-perturb for restoring plasticity. Paper [6] and [18] discuss learning-based methods for accelerating training, which partially overlap with shortened LR schedulers. Overall, the mechanism is covered across multiple papers.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves showing individual methods' effects on convergence and accuracy across CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/200, and Adaptiope. Papers [11], [15], and [19] evaluate ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets, which matches the benchmark family. Paper [16] evaluates continual learning methods on class-incremental settings, which aligns with the validation framework. Paper [14] provides empirical evidence for convergence in continual learning, which matches the statistical framework. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning/optimization for computer vision. Papers [3], [4], [13], [14], and [16] all work in continual learning, and papers [11], [15], and [19] focus on computer vision tasks. This general application area is well-covered.

**PURPOSE: Identify which optimization aspects can accelerate continual training when reusing an old model, and provide concrete first-step methods for each.**

The purpose is specifically about accelerating continual/incremental training by reusing old models (warm-starting) and decomposing the problem into optimization aspects. Paper [10] ("Step Out and Seek Around: On Warm-Start Training with Incremental Data") directly addresses warm-starting from previously trained checkpoints for incremental data scenarios to improve training efficiency. Paper [9] ("On the Difficulty of Warm-Starting Neural Network Training") also addresses the same problem of reusing old models when data arrives incrementally. Both papers pursue the same objective: making warm-start/continual training work better. This purpose is COVERED by [9] and [10].

**MECHANISM: Decompose into four aspects (initialization, regularization, data selection, hyper-parameters) with specific instantiations: shrink-and-perturb, L2-init, easy/hard replay sampling, shortened LR schedulers.**

- L2-init regularization: Papers [1] and [2] explicitly propose "L2 Init" for maintaining plasticity in continual learning — directly covered.
- Shrink-and-perturb for restoring plasticity: Paper [23] discusses plasticity loss mechanisms; paper [10] uses shrink-and-perturb explicitly for warm-starting. Paper [9] also discusses shrink-and-perturb as a baseline.
- Easy/hard replay sampling (curriculum-based data selection): Papers [17], [21] cover curriculum/difficulty-based sampling.
- Shortened LR schedulers: Paper [10] discusses learning rate schedule adjustments for warm-starting.
- The key novelty claim is the *decomposition framework* combining all four aspects. However, each individual primitive is covered. Paper [10] covers initialization (shrink-and-perturb), LR schedulers, and the warm-start framing. Papers [1]/[2] cover L2-init. The decomposition into four aspects as a unified framework is the contribution, but each mechanism is individually present. Since the question asks whether the mechanism (the technical primitive/approach) is covered, and the primitives are all present across prior papers, this is COVERED by [10], [1]/[2], [17].

**EVALUATION: Each method tested individually on CIFAR-100 (70+30) with ResNet-18; convergence acceleration shown; also tested on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/200, Adaptiope.**

The evaluation design uses standard image classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet variants) with ResNet-18, measuring convergence speed and final accuracy — a standard benchmark family used in continual learning. Paper [16] uses comprehensive empirical evaluation on continual learning with image classification benchmarks. Paper [10] evaluates warm-starting on CIFAR and ImageNet benchmarks with ResNet architectures. This evaluation design (standard vision benchmarks + ResNet + accuracy/convergence metrics in continual/incremental learning) is COVERED by [10] and [16].

**DOMAIN: Continual learning / optimization for computer vision.**

Multiple prior papers work in continual learning for computer vision image classification: [1], [2], [10], [16], [23] all operate in this exact domain. This is clearly COVERED.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to demonstrate that combining four aspects (methods) leads to large, consistent compute savings, including under repeated (multi-task) updates. None of the prior papers explicitly establish this specific empirical relationship — that the combination of methods yields consistent compute savings across tasks and updates. While some papers (e.g., [6], [14], [15], [20]) discuss aspects of continual learning, catastrophic forgetting, or multi-task learning, none report or establish the same empirical relationship about compute savings from combining methods. Therefore, **purpose is uncovered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves an empirical study that combines all first-step methods and measures speedup-to-match-scratch across datasets, class splits, and sequential multi-task settings. Paper [21] ("DeltaGrad: Rapid retraining of machine learning models") uses a similar mechanism of measuring speedup in retraining models to avoid training from scratch, which aligns with the primitive of "measuring speedup-to-match-scratch." Although the specific datasets and settings differ, the underlying mechanism of studying speedup through incremental methods is substantively equivalent. Therefore, **mechanism is covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring compute reduction (e.g., up to 2.7x on CIFAR-100, ~2.24x on CIFAR-10, etc.) to match from-scratch accuracy, as well as observing multi-task performance trends (e.g., L100 > 1 growing across tasks). Paper [21] also evaluates compute savings by comparing retraining efficiency to training from scratch, which matches the evaluation design of measuring compute reduction to achieve comparable performance. While the specific datasets and metrics differ, the evaluation design is substantively equivalent. Therefore, **evaluation is covered**.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning in computer vision. Several prior papers, such as [6], [14], [15], and [20], explicitly address continual learning in computer vision or related areas (e.g., class-incremental learning, multi-task learning). These papers operate in the same general application area, even if the specific datasets or sub-problems differ. Therefore, **domain is covered**.
